newsitem.title: GERMANY: German IG Metall union scraps talks with employers.
newsitem.headline: German IG Metall union scraps talks with employers.

text.p: German metalworkers union IG Metall on Friday cancelled a top-level meeting with employers set for Sunday on part-time working prior to retirement, citing "unbridgable differences" over pay.

Employers' federation Gesamtmetall said the decision, just days after the union demanded a further cut in the working week to 32 hours from 35, was a sign that IG Metall was opting for conflict rather than consensus.
IG Metall and employers locked horns on Friday for the second time in a week, continuing a confrontation which economists say is eroding the country's collective bargaining process.
Sunday's talks had been aimed at finding a way to phase in part-time working for older workers to help boost employment of young people.
The two sides said in separate statements they could not agree on how to pay for the system.
Employers said engineering companies could not afford IG Metall's demand for older workers to get 85 percent of net pay while working half their previous hours.
The employers were also not prepared to compensate workers for any resulting reduction in pension entitlements.
IG Metall said that against that background, there was no scope for an agreement.

"The transition to retirement and the planned move to make room for younger people must be done in a way which ensures dignity for those affected and must not lead to impoverishment at the end of one's working life," the IG Metall statement said.
Goldman Sachs senior economist Thomas Mayer said the inability of IG Metall and Gesamtmetall to resolve their differences was eroding Germany's tradition of industry-wide wage agreements.
Union membership was declining and companies were leaving their association, Mayer said.
"To find a consensus about how to fight unemployment you have to agree about its causes," Mayer said. "If you can't agree on that, the chances for agreeing how to combat the problem are very slight."

Gerhard Grebe, an economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, speculated that IG Metall might have cancelled Sunday's talks partly because it was irked by the employers' swift dismissal of the 32-hour week proposal.
The recent success of miners and construction workers in winning increased government support by striking might also have encouraged IG Metall to take a tougher line, Grebe said.

"I can imagine that after the strikes of the miners and construction workers, IG Metall senses itself in an uptrend and wants to flex its muscles," Grebe said. "It is sad. I think sensible solutions are blocked by this."

IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel proposed a further cut in the work week, accompanied by a partial reduction in wages, to help reduce German unemployment -- which in February hit the highest level since Hitler came to power in 1933.
But the employers responded by saying joblessness could not be reduced by simply making those in work work less.
